title: My Daily Brief
overview: Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO, and President Trump's claim that he arranged it, drew foreign and domestic criticism as a short-lived market rally faded and Anthropic shares fell below their IPO price. A US jury convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 counts but acquitted it of racketeering. Other stories include the Army's planned lead azide detonation in Iowa, Kilmar Abrego Garcia's departure for Spain, Rudy Giuliani's Medal of Freedom, a new Australia–Solomon Islands treaty, China's first foreign astronaut launch, and Charlotte-area news.

stories.headline: Huang's Nvidia return draws criticism as tech rally reverses
stories.summary: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after he resigned over reported affairs, including one with a woman accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent. Trump said he persuaded the board ('I convinced them... I made the deal'), and the White House said he was 'totally involved.' Huang reportedly told staff that claims of Trump's direct involvement were 'completely untrue.' Nvidia stock jumped about 30% on Monday but fell back on Tuesday, and Asian tech markets dropped sharply on Wednesday. Huang is due to testify before Congress on December 1, where Democrats plan to ask about his return and Trump's role.
key_facts: Huang resigned November 12 and was reinstated by a unanimous board vote on Monday, November 23.
Nvidia shares rose about 30–31% Monday, adding over $900 billion in market value, then fell roughly 6% Tuesday.
Taipei fell 8%, Seoul more than 5% and Tokyo more than 3% on Wednesday, after surging the day before.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Trump's intervention 'shocked me.'
Huang admitted violating Nvidia's code of conduct and said 'I made some terrible mistakes,' according to reports of an all-hands meeting.

perspectives.framing: A Guardian opinion column calls the reinstatement 'elite impunity' and an extraordinary executive-branch intervention in a private firm, stressing national security concerns and the AI bubble. The Verge focuses on Huang's all-hands meeting, where he denied Trump's role while apologising, and notes the pending congressional testimony and accounting investigation.

CNA covers the market reversal, quoting analysts who called Monday's rally a 'dead-cat bounce' amid doubts about AI returns. Deutsche Welle leads with the German foreign minister's shock and Trump's boasting, and notes an FT estimate that Trump's own Nvidia stake gained $15 million. The Hill reports frustration from lawmakers.
A Reason podcast discusses the return with 'mixed feelings,' with segments titled 'It's all political' and 'Certain tech CEOs are irreplaceable.'

disputed: Trump and the White House say he arranged Huang's return; Huang reportedly called this 'completely untrue.'
The allegation that Huang's partner was a Chinese spy, and what information may have been shared, is unproven. Nvidia's internal investigation and outside probes are ongoing.
Reports differ on Nvidia's Tuesday decline: about 6% at the close versus more than 7% at midday.
stories.why: It raises questions about government influence over a company that is central to the AI-driven stock market.

stories.headline: US jury convicts Huawei on 10 of 12 counts, acquits on racketeering
stories.summary: A federal jury in Brooklyn found Huawei and three subsidiaries guilty of charges including conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank and wire fraud, and sanctions violations. Jurors acquitted the company of racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice. Prosecutors said Huawei spent two decades lying to banks about its Iran business and stealing technology from firms including Cisco and T-Mobile. Huawei called the racketeering acquittal vindication, said the remaining charges lack merit, and plans to appeal. Sentencing is set for September 14, 2027.
key_facts: Guilty on 10 of 12 counts; acquitted of racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice.
Victim companies included Cisco, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile, Quintel USA and Fujitsu, according to court records.
Attorney General Todd Blanche: 'For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft.'
Sentencing is scheduled for September 14, 2027, with possible fines, forfeiture and restitution.
Charges were first disclosed in 2019, after Meng Wanzhou's 2018 arrest in Canada.

perspectives.framing: PBS (AP) and The Verge give both prosecutors' examples of theft and the defence's argument that isolated misconduct was spun into a grand conspiracy. PBS adds China's 'economic bullying' charge and Huawei's continued global growth, including in AI chips.

BBC, DW and CNBC present it as a mixed verdict, quoting DOJ officials alongside Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig. CNBC highlights DOJ details such as engineers spelling Cisco backward and surveillance cameras supplied to Iran.

The Daily Caller stresses the convictions and the scope of the theft allegations, notes Huawei's denial of ties to the Chinese Communist Party, and links the case to a Commerce Department action related to the Huang scandal.

disputed: Huawei says the five trade-secret disputes were civil matters resolved years ago; prosecutors say they show a pattern of crime.
Outlets describe the trial's length differently: two months, 11 weeks, or three months.
The Daily Caller says a heavy penalty 'has been set'; other outlets say penalties will be decided at sentencing in 2027.
stories.why: The verdict is a major legal milestone in US–China tech tensions, and appeals are expected.

stories.headline: Charlotte DA drops rental-car charge against Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack
stories.summary: Mecklenburg County District Attorney Spencer Merriweather dismissed, with prejudice, a felony charge against Democratic Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack over a rental car she failed to return in 2019. Womack paid Budget the overdue rental cost, and the company said it did not want to prosecute. The 2020 summons was served during an October campaign event. Womack, who said she was homeless at the time, defeated Republican Rep. Tim Moore and will be sworn in in January.
key_facts: The car was rented August 27, 2019, renewed twice, and recovered by police December 4, 2019.
A criminal summons was issued January 14, 2020, and served in October 2026.
The dismissal was filed with prejudice after full restitution.
Womack won North Carolina's 14th District.

perspectives.framing: WFAE notes the publicity did not hurt her campaign and places her win within a 'blue wave' in which Democrats took 11 of 14 state seats.

Local TV outlets and The Hill lay out the DA's timeline and the settlement. WSOC includes her account of being homeless. Axios calls her a 'wave baby' who unexpectedly won a heavily Republican district.

stories.why: It removes a legal cloud over an incoming member of Congress before she takes office.

stories.headline: China launches Shenzhou-24 carrying first foreign astronaut to Tiangong
stories.summary: China's Shenzhou-24 lifted off from Jiuquan on Wednesday with commander Tang Hongbo, flight engineer Wu Yi and Pakistani pilot Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to fly on a Chinese crewed mission. Ali will spend about 5 to 10 days on the Tiangong station conducting experiments before returning with two departing Shenzhou-23 crew members. Shenzhou-23 commander Zhu Yangzhu will stay aboard for a year to study how the body copes in space. China says its 2030 crewed moon landing target is unchanged.
key_facts: Launched at 8:18 a.m. local time on a Long March-2F rocket.
Ali, 40, trained for seven months in Beijing.
The crew plans more than 90 experiments and technology tests, according to Xinhua.
Pakistani PM Shehbaz Sharif called the flight 'a historic first.'

perspectives.framing: Al Jazeera gives a brief report focused on Ali and his biotech and materials-science work under a China–Pakistan agreement.

Reuters (via the Korea Herald), DW and BBC cover the crew, the unusual handover and the year-long stay, placing the launch in the US–China moon race. Reuters notes Washington's warnings about lunar resources and Beijing's denial.

stories.why: It signals China's push to make Tiangong a hub for international partners as the ISS nears retirement.

stories.headline: Army set to detonate five tons of lead azide in Iowa amid health concerns
stories.summary: The Army planned to detonate about five tons of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday morning, after a federal appeals court lifted a stay. Army officials say the crystallised explosive risks detonating on its own, and that a controlled, mitigated blast is far safer. Residents, environmental groups and state officials criticised poor communication about a toxic lead dust plume projected to drift southwest into Missouri. Gov. Kim Reynolds backed the plan, declared a disaster emergency in three counties and deployed up to 100 National Guard soldiers.
key_facts: 68 barrels, about five tons, scheduled for around 9 a.m. CST (10 a.m. ET) Wednesday.
An Army inspection on March 11, 2026, found the lead azide had partially crystallised.
Alerts told people within 20 miles to stay indoors; some within 5 miles southwest may be evacuated, with FEMA support.
The Eighth Circuit lifted a stay and denied an emergency pause; earlier dates of November 20 and 23 slipped.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian, PBS and Vox stress communication failures, the fact that no level of lead exposure is safe, and residents' alarm, quoting Sen.-elect Josh Turek. They also give the Army's 'least bad option' argument. Vox says Trump tried to shift the decision to incoming Democratic Gov. Rob Sand.
Newsweek centres on Army mitigation and the 1977 Colorado precedent, as described by an officer. The Hill emphasises the governor's support despite unresolved safety questions.

The Daily Caller focuses on the new plume maps and the Army and DOJ case for urgency, including the risk of cold weather and removed blast doors. It notes Trump ordered a halt pending the court ruling and the incoming governor's input.

disputed: How far the plume could travel is unclear: one estimate cited by Vox puts it at up to 100 miles.
Questions remain about why other disposal methods weren't used.
Newsweek attributes the 1977 remarks to a 'Col. Aaron Teller,' while other outlets quote acting Army Secretary Adam Telle; it is unclear whether these are the same person.
stories.why: Thousands of people face possible lead exposure on one of the year's busiest holiday weeks.

stories.headline: Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves the US for Spain under sealed agreement
stories.summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whose March 2025 deportation to El Salvador the administration called an 'administrative error,' boarded a flight to Madrid on Tuesday under an agreement with federal authorities. The terms remain sealed. The departure avoids a planned removal to an African country such as Liberia. Sen. Chris Van Hollen said he was leaving as 'a free man,' and his lawyers said he plans to go on to Mexico. The DOJ is still appealing the dismissal of human smuggling charges against him in Tennessee.
key_facts: He was deported to El Salvador in March 2025 despite a 2019 order barring removal there, then returned in June 2025.
Judge Waverly Crenshaw dismissed the Tennessee smuggling charges in May, finding reason to believe the prosecution was vindictive.
Judge Paula Xinis issued a sealed order Friday.
Abrego Garcia had offered to go to Costa Rica; a former ICE acting director pushed for Liberia instead.

perspectives.framing: Al Jazeera leads with Van Hollen's praise and details the CECOT detention, the 'administrative error' and the ICE memo rejecting Costa Rica.
The Hill reports Van Hollen's confirmation and ABC's account of the flight.

The Washington Examiner and Daily Caller describe him as the face of Trump's deportation fight. They report his lawyers' 'vindictive prosecution' statement and the DOJ appeal, note that the judges are Obama appointees, and the Daily Caller links to DOJ allegations of MS-13 ties.

disputed: The terms of the agreement are sealed.
The DOJ's gang allegations are unproven, and the smuggling case is on appeal.
Whether a judge directed him to leave is reported through an unnamed AP source.
stories.why: It closes a high-profile test case over due process in the administration's deportation policy.

stories.headline: Trump awards Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom
stories.summary: Trump presented former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani, 82, with the Presidential Medal of Freedom in a closed-press White House ceremony on Tuesday. The White House cited his leadership after 9/11. Giuliani later served as Trump's lawyer in efforts to overturn the 2020 election and was disbarred in New York and Washington. Giuliani said he was 'honored and humbled.'
key_facts: Trump first announced the award last year, after Giuliani was seriously injured in a car crash.
Giuliani was disbarred over false statements about the 2020 election.
Former election workers Ruby Freeman and Shaye Moss were involved in a $148 million defamation case against him.
Other second-term medals include posthumous awards to Charlie Kirk and Welles Crowther.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian and PBS pair the 9/11 legacy with his disbarment, defamation case, bankruptcy and 2020 election role. They note the press was excluded and quote his son praising his legal work.
The Hill focuses on the 9/11 'America's Mayor' legacy and the White House's praise.
A New York Post column calls the award well deserved, treats the 2020 controversies as 'footnotes,' and highlights his record as a crime-fighting prosecutor and mayor.

disputed: Outlets describe the $148 million case differently: PBS says the workers won a judgment, while the Guardian and NY Post describe a settlement (the Post says it was settled before trial).
stories.why: The award highlights sharply divided views of Giuliani's legacy and of Trump's use of national honours.

stories.headline: Solomon Islands signs security treaty with Australia, moving away from China pact
stories.summary: Solomon Islands PM Matthew Wale and Australian PM Anthony Albanese signed a treaty in Canberra making Australia the country's primary security partner. It bars foreign military bases and requires consultation with Australia on critical infrastructure and on security deals outside the Pacific Islands Forum. Reports say Honiara will not renew its 2022 security pact with China. Wale said talks with Beijing are 'ongoing' and cited a non-disclosure clause. China said its Pacific ties involve no 'geopolitical contests or bloc confrontation.'
key_facts: Wale: 'Solomon Islands has been... a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region... Those days are gone.'
The Guardian reports $740 million in Australian funding over 10 years ($670 million in grants, $70 million in loans).
Sensitive infrastructure is to remain 'free from militarisation, foreign interference and unauthorised access.'
About 14 Chinese police officers are expected to leave by mid-2027, according to the Guardian.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian calls it a blow to China and a win for Albanese, details the funding, education, visa and labour programmes, and anticipates a backlash from Beijing.

AFP (via the Korea Herald) and BBC describe it as countering China, quoting Lowy Institute and Crisis Group analysts. AFP notes Wale's fragile hold on power and that parliament has been adjourned, raising questions about how long the deal will last.

disputed: Whether the China pact has formally been terminated: Wale won't confirm, and China neither confirmed nor denied.
The pact's expiry date is given as April or April 2027.
How long the deal will last given Wale's political position.
stories.why: It reshapes the US–China–Australia contest for influence in the Pacific.

stories.headline: Anthropic shares fall below $83 IPO price
stories.summary: Anthropic stock fell about 12–13% on Tuesday to around $76, below its $83 IPO price, less than a week after debuting at $111.50. The decline came as Nvidia gave back part of Monday's gains. Options trading shows traders are split on what comes next. Analysts say the stock's performance could affect valuations and IPO plans for other AI startups.
key_facts: IPO price $83; opening trade $111.50; intraday high $115.
The stock fell under its IPO price in four trading days.
The offering raised $91.6 billion before fees.
Computing costs took 58 cents of every revenue dollar in Q3, up from 48 cents, according to its filing.

perspectives.framing: CNBC focuses on options activity and mixed trader sentiment. TechCrunch frames the drop as a worrying signal for AI startup valuations and IPOs.
The Daily Caller emphasises investor losses and questions whether AI spending will turn into profit, citing rising compute costs and $70.7 billion in commitments.

disputed: Reported size of the drop varies: nearly 12%, 13%, or 13.1%.
stories.why: Anthropic is widely watched as a test of how public markets value AI companies.

stories.headline: Coastal storm could disrupt Thanksgiving travel in the Carolinas
stories.summary: A developing coastal storm, expected to become a nor'easter, is forecast to bring rain and strong winds to the Carolinas from Wednesday evening into Thanksgiving morning, clearing by Black Friday. The FAA warned that rain could affect flights across the Southeast on one of the busiest travel days. Pacific storms are also hitting the West Coast.
key_facts: AAA projects 81.5 million Americans will travel 50+ miles between November 24 and 30.
The FAA says weather has caused 60% of delays this year.
The heaviest rain is expected Wednesday night into Thursday morning.

perspectives.framing: Local stations and the BBC give practical forecasts and travel advice, including traveller interviews and airport notification plans.

investigations.question: What is happening with AI regulation in the US and EU?
investigations.update: No articles this edition addressed US or EU AI regulation. One analyst in the Nvidia coverage cited 'the threat of regulation under a new administration from next year' as a risk for the AI sector.
